name: Basecamp
subcategory: team projects, issues and delivery planning
tagline: Organize projects around messages, to-dos, files, schedules, and check-ins

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 1 project, 1 GB storage, up to 20 users

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Unlimited projects, 500 GB storage; clients, guests and contractors are free, while employees are paid seats

tiers.name: Pro Unlimited
tiers.limits: Unlimited users/projects, 5 TB storage and priority support

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 project, 1 GB storage and up to 20 users
pricing.billingTerms: Free + Pro monthly only + Pro Unlimited annual only; trials require no card and do not auto-charge
pricing.hiddenCosts: On Pro, every employee is a $15/month seat; only clients/guests/contractors are free. Optional Timesheet, Admin Pro Pack and each extra 1 TB of storage cost $50/month apiece. Pro Unlimited requires the full annual commitment, though cancellation refunds unused annual time pro rata.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Basecamp, organize projects around messages, to-dos, files, schedules, and check-ins. The hard boundary is mature opinionated workflow, email delivery, guest access, support, and reliability, plus collaboration, integrations, and organizational trust.
coreLoopDIY: Organize projects around messages, to-dos, files, schedules, and check-ins, with comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
whatYouLose: mature opinionated workflow, email delivery, guest access, support, and reliability
ongoingBurden: auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Basecamp because teams pay because project state has to remain authoritative through staff changes, outages, and years of accumulated workflow exceptions. The recurring cost buys auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Plane
priorArt.desc: Active open-source project and issue tracking platform.

alternatives.name: ONLYOFFICE Groups
alternatives.desc: Projects, discussions, files, calendars, milestones, and time tracking in one enormous self-hosted office

facts.install: Deploy the official ONLYOFFICE Community Server Docker image, normally alongside Document Server and Mail Server as needed
facts.dataFormat: Groupware records live in the deployment's relational database and users' documents/attachments live on persistent server storage; Docker deployments mount host directories for data, logs, and configuration.
facts.gapVsPaid: ONLYOFFICE Groups replaces Basecamp's deliberate calm with an enormous office suite whose setup, permissions, and menus are far more complex and whose automatic check-ins are less central.
facts.setupBlocker: The product is an office suite rather than a small project app: a usable deployment brings Docker, persistent volumes, a database, domains/TLS, mail settings, and often separate Document Server services.

alternatives.name: Huly
alternatives.desc: Tasks, docs, chat, calendar, and files; hosted Huly died in July, so this is self-host or nothing

facts.install: Run the official Huly Selfhost Docker Compose stack on Linux, using its setup script plus Nginx/TLS for production
facts.dataFormat: The self-host stack uses CockroachDB for account/workspace data, Elasticsearch for search indexes, Redpanda for event streams, and persistent volumes for uploaded files; optional services may add MongoDB. The public hosted Huly service announced its shutdown, so new use means self-hosting.
facts.gapVsPaid: Huly's hosted service is gone and its self-hosted issue-doc-chat stack is more technical and less client-friendly than Basecamp's simple project spaces, check-ins, and email participation.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is the production-sized stack: Linux, Docker Compose, Nginx and certificates plus CockroachDB, Redpanda, Elasticsearch, storage volumes, backups, and enough RAM.

alternatives.name: OpenProject
alternatives.desc: To-dos, files, schedules, meetings, forums, and wikis; calm is not included

facts.install: Hosted Enterprise Cloud signup, or Community Edition via Docker Compose/all-in-one Docker or supported Linux packages
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted application data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded attachments live on a persistent filesystem volume or configured S3-compatible object storage, while configuration and any linked repositories must be backed up separately. Cloud data lives in OpenProject's hosted infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: OpenProject can hold files, meetings, forums, and schedules, but its enterprise planning interface is much less approachable than Basecamp for ordinary clients and small teams.
facts.setupBlocker: The free Community Edition needs a Linux server; the recommended Docker setup still requires persistent database/file volumes, a hostname, TLS, and mail configuration.

alternatives.name: Leantime
alternatives.desc: Projects, discussions, files, milestones, and status reporting without Basecamp's deliberate simplicity

facts.install: Paid hosted signup, or the free open-source edition via Docker Compose/official image or a PHP release archive plus MySQL/MariaDB
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted project data lives in MySQL 8 or MariaDB 10.6+, while uploaded files use the local filesystem or configured S3-compatible storage; hosted-account data lives in Leantime's cloud.
facts.gapVsPaid: Leantime has projects, discussions, milestones, and status reports, but its communication flow, mobile polish, email participation, and automatic check-ins are weaker than Basecamp's.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no longer a permanent free hosted tier: the free route means operating PHP, MySQL/MariaDB, persistent storage, backups, and a web-facing Docker or LAMP stack.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Plus plan and a small-team tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Basecamp in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: organize projects around messages, to-dos, files, schedules, and check-ins, with comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement organizations, projects, members, issues, labels, cycles, and milestones.
Provide list, kanban, and simple timeline views backed by one canonical issue model.
Add comments, mentions, assignments, watchers, and a complete activity log.
Implement project roles for owner, member, and viewer and test every mutation.
Add search, CSV import or export, email notifications, and daily database backups.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, migrations, seed data, and an admin recovery command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of external integrations.
Deliberately leave out enterprise portfolio planning and SSO.
Deliberately leave out native mobile clients and vendor-operated uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
